No event was declared. Money publishes `payment.succeeded@1` for a group's charge as for any payment, and nothing else
acts on a group, a membership or a claim that was never sent; an event nobody but its publisher acts on is refused by
the event contract. `claim.submitted@2` and `claim.decided@1` stay frozen and unpublished, for the day a partner exists.

Still open: no group pays for a plan or a medicine collection, only a visit; a group's own payment method is the
provider's page and no mandate is modelled; a treasurer sees her members by the names she invited them under, which the
preview holds and no route carries; the pre-authorisation frame is a frame only — Movement owns
`admission.preauth.submitted@1`, so Money builds no route for one; a claim is never re-drafted after a visit is
refunded; the Banks Act reading behind "no pooled money" and what a group's charge is under the National Payment
System Act have not been put to counsel; and the employer suppression floor is the programmes' judgement, which no
Information Officer has agreed to. (`gifts@1` and `market-orders@1` were built in Wave 6, below.)

## Delivered — an Encounter's signature and supersede, and the status route Care was waiting on, 16 September 2026 (Wave 6, Record)

`GET /v1/record/encounter-statuses/{encounterRef}@1` stayed proposed at Wave 5 because the Passport stored no
signature and no supersede (`packages/catalog/hl7v2-inbound.json` `encounters.encounterStatuses`, and the "What
stays open" note in the HL7 bridge section above). This wave built the storage the route needed, then the route
on top of it — nothing else. **The route now answers `built`**, and `encounters.encounterStatuses.decision` in
`hl7v2-inbound.json` says so.

| What landed                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           | The refusals it adds                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              | Where                                                                                                                  |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **`encounter_states`, a lifecycle table for one resource type.** Every other resource is written once per version, unchanged; an Encounter specifically now carries a state — written, signed or superseded — in a row of its own keyed by the resource id, inserted once and moved at most once more: `signEncounterState` and `supersedeEncounterState` each fire only from `written`, so a second sign or a supersede of something already signed or superseded changes nothing. Superseding never touches the old resource's own row — a supersede is a new resource replacing the old one by reference, and the old one is kept exactly as it was signed or read | none of its own; a break in either one-way move is caught by the boundary check below rather than by a test that happens to look afterwards                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       | `apps/passport/src/store.ts`                                                                                           |
| **`writeEncounter` and `signEncounter`, gateway methods with no HTTP route of their own yet.** A nurse's or a doctor's own grant files an Encounter (never the patient's own session — an Encounter is what a clinician found, not what the patient reported); `supersedes` names the entry it replaces. Only the assigned doctor's own grant signs one, never the nurse who wrote it. Neither is routed over HTTP: no engine reaches the Passport that way today (`packages/engines/src/record/engine.ts`'s own header names the gap), so both are exercised directly, exactly as `write()` already is in every other Passport test                                  | `write-not-permitted` (the patient, or a grant that does not write); `out-of-scope` (a grant outside the admission category); `sign-requires-a-doctor`; `encounter-already-signed` (signing a signed one again, or superseding a signed one — signed is corrected by a new entry, never replaced, echoing Clinical's own `signed-is-immutable` for the review rather than the entry beneath it); `encounter-already-superseded` (signing or superseding one already superseded); `no-such-encounter` (a `supersedes` reference that is not a written Encounter of this subject's) | `apps/passport/src/gateway.ts`                                                                                         |

| **Tests and the boundary check.** Passport `node:test`: written; written then signed; v1 superseded by v2, pointing forward; signing a superseded version; superseding a signed version; double-sign and double-supersede; an unknown reference against a reference of a different kind, compared byte for byte; a resource with no state beside it; who may write and sign; every transition in the patient's own `/audit/mine`. A boundary check exercises the same gateway — not a shortcut — for the one-way moves, the unchanged resource row, the identical refusal body and the HL7 hook, each proven to fire by breaking its source and restored              | `apps/passport/test/encounter-status.test.ts`, `apps/passport/test/server.test.ts`, the Record · Encounter signature and supersede block at the end of `scripts/check-boundaries.mjs`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |

No screen was built. Nothing on any platform reads this route today: Care's own engine has no call path to the
Passport (the same gap `packages/engines/src/record/engine.ts` already names for the HL7 bridge's hand-off), and
the web's Clinical workspace already shows a doctor's signature on _the review_ — `ClinicalWorkbench.tsx`'s
`consultation.signedAt`, from Clinical's own `review.signed@1` — which is a different signature about a different
thing. `review.signed@1`'s payload (`reviewRef`, `encounterRef`, `signedByRef`) and its `neverCarries` list
(assessment, diagnosis, clinical notes, red flags, patient identity — all Clinical's own consultation, staying in
Clinical's own store) say it signs Clinical's review of an encounter, never the Passport's Encounter resource
itself; Money's claim already reads the same distinction the other way, finding a signed review through
`review.billable@1` and never through a `reviewRef` on a route (the group payers and claims section above). So
signing here is Passport-local, on the doctor's own grant, and stays that way until a route calls it: wiring
Clinical's signature to also sign the Passport's Encounter would conflate two different signatures — a clinician's
decision about their review, and a record-keeping state about the entry underneath it — and would need the
engine-to-Passport call path to exist first, which is a larger piece than one route.

## Delivered — Core's four remaining structural routes, 16 September 2026 (seed plan, Wave 6, Core)

The four routes `packages/catalog/apis/core.json` had left proposed since Wave 2: the event bus's own
front door, the protocol registry's read, its ratify route, a role × scope × purpose check and an
audit export. None carries clinical content and none needed a supplier. **The ratify route never
ratifies anything**: its one caller, `medical-director`, is not a role the vetting register has
cleared anybody into, so it refuses every call with the registry's own sentence for a ratification
with no name behind it — the correct behaviour today, not a stub.

## Delivered — households, sponsorships and bill splits, 16 September 2026 (seed plan, Wave 6, Access)

The three arrangements a family makes around one person's care, and the one thing none of them is. A household is a
**roster** and grants nobody access to anybody's record; a sponsor **pays and reads nothing about the care**; a bill
split is one payable cut into shares **each payer accepts for themselves**. Three routes were declared in Wave 2 and
never built; two of them could not be built as written and are withdrawn and versioned.

| What landed                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        | The refusals it adds                                                                                                                                           | Where                                                               |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **A household roster** (`POST /v1/access/households@1`, built as it was frozen; `POST /v1/access/household-memberships@1` adds a line; `GET /v1/access/households@1` reads one). A membership holds four things — the household, the member, who added them and the day — and there is no field for a scope, a purpose, an expiry or a relationship, because each of those is half of a consent grant. **Listing somebody grants nothing to them and nothing to the person who added them**                                        | `membership-is-not-consent` on both writes; `not-in-this-household` on reading a roster and on adding to one — who lives with whom is a fact about all of them | `household.json`, `access/domain/household.ts`, `Household.tsx`     |
| **A request that tries to attach a grant to a roster line is refused rather than ignored.** The routes declare no such field, so an attempt arrives undeclared; the binder hands the handler the _names_ of what was sent, and the words are read from `household.json` `grantFieldWords`. A dropped field is a field somebody believes worked                                                                                                                                                                                     | `membership-is-not-consent`, on the words `scope`, `grant`, `permission`, `consent`, `access`, `expires` and the rest                                          | `household.ts` `namesAGrant`                                        |
| **A sponsorship names a household membership, never a typed name** (`POST /v1/access/sponsors@2`; version one withdrawn: it took a subject reference and nothing else, so a sponsorship could be opened against any string, and it had nowhere for the recipient's agreement to live). It starts **offered** and moves only when the person being paid for answers in her own account (`…/answer@1`), which is what `programmes.json` has always said                                                                              | `not-a-household-member`, `sponsor-reads-nothing`, `only-the-recipient-answers`, `answer-not-offered`                                                          | `access/domain/sponsorship.ts`, `Sponsor.tsx`                       |

## Delivered — GilbertOne phase 1: the character demonstrator, 17 September 2026 (web only)

A rig, a widget shell and a control for every cue in `docs/GilbertOne_Developer_Scope_v1.md`'s animation tables, so the
motion in that scope can be reviewed before any of the decisions behind it are made. **This is a preview of GilbertOne's
presentation, not GilbertOne itself.** It previews look and animation only: the live assistant — `packages/catalog/assistant.json`'s
matcher, its descriptor line and the voice policy the founder set on 14 September — is unchanged, and this page is wired
to none of it. This is phase 1 of the scope's four, and the other three are gated on decisions this repository has not
made: a pinned model checkpoint, a speech provider and a clinical review of care content.

It is reached at `/app/?preview=gilbertone`, and from nowhere else: no navigation, menu or link in the product points
at it. **Open on the deployed site since 17 September**, having been development-only until that day — `src/Doorway.tsx`
wrote the door against `import.meta.env.DEV` and no longer does. The page did not change when the door did: the preview
badge, every refusal notice and the voice capability's own words are the same, and it still reaches no network, no
microphone and no browser media API of any kind. The patient pays **0.15 kB gzipped** for the door itself — 275.57 kB
before and 275.72 kB after, across the same 13 files, measured the way this file measures everything. Everything behind
it is a dynamic import: the demonstrator, the rig, the widget, the manifest and the two contracts it quotes are
**15.42 kB of JavaScript and 2.61 kB of CSS, gzipped**, and none of it is fetched until the address is opened.

## Delivered — a microphone on the live web assistant, decided 18 September 2026, landed 19 September (web only)

The founder widened the browser route §07 built on the demonstrator to the shipped assistant, so that a patient who
cannot type can speak her question instead. The reason it was refused on 14 September has not been overturned — a
browser's recognition may send what a person said to the company that makes the browser — so the decision is answered
with a disclosure rather than a retraction: `voice.web` is `true`, `voice.webRecognition` is `browser`, and
`voice.webDecision` carries `decidedBy`, `on`, `why` and `reverses` beside them. The build fails if the field and the
decision that justifies it disagree, or if either is missing, which is the gap that let the control reach a patient
page ahead of the paperwork: the gate's own staleness guard had quietly stopped running the day the change went in,

## Delivered — the character on the live assistant panel, decided 19 September 2026 (web only, phase 1 of one GilbertOne)

The founder's "one GilbertOne" decision of 19 September begins with its first phase: the robot rig the demonstrator
proved replaces the sphere on the panel a patient actually meets, and the sphere is deleted rather than left standing
as a second character. The work is the seam, not the character — the panel already spoke `pulse` and the rig already
spoke cues, and the translation between them is one effect: an escalation holds A16's steady urgent face, a handover
holds A11's attentive one, and every completed turn otherwise buys A09's single nod, which is what `gatheredAt`
crossed the seam to buy. Opening still greets with A01 once, and a re-open onto a conversation in progress reads its
last message (A05) — the widget's own rule, now honest under React's double-invoked development mount, whose second
run used to play the re-open cue on a first open and, on the activity track, refuse the first reply's nod for a full
second.

## Delivered — the character's affect, decided 19 September 2026 (web only, phase 2 of one GilbertOne)

The founder's "one GilbertOne" decision said affect is deterministic and derived from the answer kind
alone — no model — and its second phase makes that a contract: a dated `affect` section beside the
matcher whose answers it maps, giving every answer kind a cue and a posture. The situations wear A13's
brief warm smile (warm), the identity and voice answers wear A17's flat face while their refusals are
stated (flat), the emergency holds A16's steady face (flat), unmatched and a turn with unread words
wear A12's lifted brow (concerned), and the handover holds A11's smaller smile (attentive). The
founder's own four words — routine to warm, refusal to flat, unmatched to concerned, emergency to
A16 — are pinned by the build, and the kinds are derived from the contract itself: a new answer kind
added to `questions` or `answers` without a face fails `npm run check` the day it is added.

The panel no longer chooses a face. `cueOf` reads the reply's kind from the contract, with the
unread override the section itself explains: a turn whose words could not be read wears the concerned
face whatever else it matched, because the unread block in that turn is a refusal. The posture is
read off the cue that owns the face, so the readable `data-affect` cannot say warm over a face A16 is
holding. And the invariant that outranks everything else — **affect may never soften a refusal or an
emergency** — is enforced by running the rig's real reducer inside `scripts/check-boundaries.mjs`,
not by paraphrasing its rules: A16 takes the flat face from a held attentive pose and keeps it against
every other cue in the manifest, from later turns and from stale ones, on the animated path and under
reduced motion, through every step and through settling, and only Start again — the patient's own
reset — rests it.

| What landed                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            | What it refuses                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              | Where                                            |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| **The affect section as data** — every answer kind with a `cue`, a `posture` and a written `why`; the greeting idiom (`openFirst` once, `openAgain` on a re-open, the blink and idle drift named as additive channels that never own the face); and eight dormant cues in `notWired`, each with the reason it is not wired                                                                                             | The founder's four words pinned: routine warm, refusal flat, unmatched concerned, emergency the one cue on the safety track — held, flat, undisplaceable. The posture vocabulary is closed at four words and each is honest against the cue it names — warm needs a smile, flat a flat mouth, concerned a lifted brow, attentive a tilt — and never warm over the five refusal-bearing kinds | `packages/catalog/assistant.json` `affect`       |
| **The seam asks the contract.** `cueOf` maps the kind — unread overriding the match — and `postureOf` reads the posture off the running cue; the greeting effect plays the conversation cues; the panel types no cue id of its own                                                                                                                                                                                     | A boundary check fails on a typed cue id in the panel or the lib, on a greeting not read from `affect.conversation`, on a posture not read off the rig's running cue, and on the panel calling the rig's `stop` — the words and the face cannot drift apart because neither is written twice                                                                                                 | `lib/assistant.ts`, `Assistant.tsx`              |
| **The never-soften invariant, proven by the reducer itself.** The gate imports the rig over node's type-stripping and runs `reduce`: A16 holds against all sixteen other cues from later and stale turns on both motion paths, through advance and settle; an emergency takes the face from a held A11; only `rest` releases it. Sixteen ways of breaking the guarded sources were tried and every one fails the build | Every cue in the manifest is accounted for — wired, conversation, or `notWired` with a reason — so a cue cannot appear on the face that no contract sentence explains                                                                                                                                                                                                                        | `scripts/check-boundaries.mjs`, the affect block |
| **The spec reads the contract, not the manifest.** `faceOf(kind)` holds each kind to its own cue and posture on both viewports — the greeting on open and re-open, the warm situation, the two flat refusals, the concerned unmatched and unread, the held emergency, the attentive handover, and Start again releasing cue and posture together                                                                       | Phase 1's typed A09/A11/A16 assertions are retired with the mapping, because the face is the contract's now; A13's smile is a gesture, so it is asserted at once before it settles; and under reduced motion the emergency still holds its flat face, because a still face can still be an urgent one. 46 journeys pass and 4 skip by design — a phone's arithmetic                          | `tests/assistant.spec.ts`                        |

**What did not move.** The rig itself: no cue, timing, track or priority order in `lib/gilbertone.ts`
changed — the file's import specifiers gained the extensions node's type-stripping needs, which is
what lets the gate run the real reducer instead of a copy of its rules. The three decisions the
founder closed stay closed: no model — the same answer wears the same face every time because the
face is data; roles demo-scoped and labelled simulated until the identity service exists; speech
built behind a contract flag and off, with A10 in `notWired` saying so. The phones are untouched —
`emit-assistant.mjs` deliberately emits none of this, because cue ids are the web rig's vocabulary
and iOS and Android keep the six states the 17 September renaming left them — and the demonstrator
keeps its own rig, its own greeting idiom and its own tests.

**The affect costs the patient's entry nothing, measured rather than presumed.** The entry was built
and measured with this change stashed and with it applied: 282.62 kB across the same 13 files, byte
for byte identical both ways, because the contract rides the assistant's lazy import and the entry's
asset list does not mention it. That the tree stands 0.46 kB over the 282.16 kB CLAUDE.md records
from `8bf3e48` is therefore not this change's doing — it came with the work that landed between 16
and 19 September (the live assistant's microphone, the engine bridge, the panel fixes, the rig
itself), and whether it is accepted or taken back is the founder's decision, not a line item to
absorb quietly.

## Delivered — the second tier's production gate, 21 September 2026 (bridge live, service dark)

The web panel's bridge to GilbertOne's second tier had shipped ahead of its paperwork: a service behind it with a wildcard CORS header, an unguarded paid endpoint, a consent line that still said no model ever receives what a person says, and a permissions header still refusing the microphone the live assistant was given on 19 September. This pass closes each of those where it was open, and makes the second tier something a deploy can deliver in full without ever switching it on. All four states it can be in — **bridge shipped**, **runtime installed but disabled**, **provider configured**, and **production operational** — are named apart in `deploy/RUNBOOK.md`, `deploy/README.md` and `docs/PRIVACY-AND-SECURITY.md`, because each is a different answer to "is it working".

It is a deliberate, recorded exception to `docs/PROMPT-CONTROL-TOWER-UI.md` §1 and §12 for one caller and two keys; every other screen, key and person is held to them unchanged. `docs/governance/FOUNDER-ACCESS.md` is the account, attacker by attacker.

## Next UI increments

Remaining before a pilot-ready design: the vetting reviewer console on native, which is web-only
today — and which now has a server behind it, so the console is a surface rather than a design.

**A stranger downloads the assistant's kitchen.** The landing page's own entry is 123 kB gzipped and
its pictures 275 kB, but the built first view measures ≈ 1.8 MB raw because `PublicAssistant` imports
`lib/assistant.ts`, and that module reaches the settings, studio, medicines, booking and SOS chunks —
≈ 1.2 MB the public page never renders. The fix is a split of `lib/assistant.ts` so the signed-out
sheet reads the public scope alone; until then the 26 September reduction is measured with that
chunk in the figure rather than without it.

**A clinician downloads the patient application.** Merging the entries cost a nurse 87 kB gzipped,
because `src/Doorway.tsx` imports the patient app statically — it is what `/app/` means with no role
on it, and making it lazy would put a fallback in front of every patient load and 5.8 kB on it. The
fix that costs neither is to split the patient's _own_ screens behind their own dynamic imports:
the booking flow, the passport, the household record and the emergency pathway are not on the
overview and need not be in its first load. `tests/states.spec.ts` carries the ratchet and the two
numbers. The booking flow went first, on 15 September with Wave 3's person step: it and the visit
thread are dynamic imports now, a boundary check fails if `App.tsx` imports `features/Booking`
statically, and the patient's first load measured 316.61 kB against 319.97 the same way. The emergency
pathway went second, on 15 September with Wave 4's press and next of kin: `features/Sos` and
`features/NextOfKin` are dynamic imports from `App.tsx`, and while the pathway downloads its fallback is
the emergency numbers themselves, read by name from `sos.json`, so the numbers never wait for the
download. The household record went third, on 16 September with Wave 6's roster: `features/Household` and
`features/Sponsor` are dynamic imports from `App.tsx`, a boundary check fails if either is imported statically,
and the patient's first load measured 281.39 kB against 295.49 the same way — 14 kB off a screen opened from
inside a dialog. The passport is still in it.

**Two quarantined copies are left of nine, and both retire themselves.** Moving three bodies of
prose into the catalogue could not finish in one pass, because adopting a contract means editing the
file that holds the old copy and other people had those trees open. So each copy is held to every
sentence of the contract, word for word, and its quarantine line is written to expire: an entry
whose file has _stopped_ carrying the prose is an error too, so the day a file reads the generated
data the build fails until somebody deletes the line. Seven have now done exactly that. Four iOS
copies adopted their contracts on 10 September — `Explain.swift`, `Arrival.swift`,
`CaptureQueueView.swift` and `VisitQueueView.swift` — and two Android ones followed the same day,
`Explain.kt` and `Arrival.kt`. Waiting are `CaptureQueue.kt` and the web's `VisitQueue.tsx`.

`CaptureQueue.kt` owes two sentences more than it did: `refusalFor` types the full-disk and
unexplained-refusal copy that `durability.writeFailures` holds, and it retires by reading
`CaptureData.writeFailure("disk-full")` and `("write-refused")`. Those two sentences are not in the
contract yet, which is the one piece of this that is a task rather than a deletion.

**The money and identity seams are simulated on the web only, and sign-up still types its code.**
The three stand-ins are read by the browser and by `node:test`; neither native app has a door onto
them, so iOS and Android render the simulation notices from the generated contract and go on drawing
the states behind them. And the sign-up flow's verification step still checks `code === '240924'` on
all three platforms — it is one of the demo codes a boundary check holds identical across them, so
adopting the simulated office there is a change to three applications rather than to one.

**Three lists of what is still missing, and each fails the build when it stops being missing.**
Beside the quarantines above, `scripts/check-boundaries.mjs` carries `FIGURE_QUARANTINE` (the
workspace figures still typed over a list that could count them), `SILENT_ABOUT_WRITE_FAILURE` (the
two iOS file queues with no sentence for a phone with no room left) and `SILENT_ABOUT_QUARANTINE`
(Android's reading ledger, which sets an unreadable file aside without telling the nurse where it
went). None of the three is a licence: each names what would retire it, and each is an error the day
it is no longer true.

`FIGURE_QUARANTINE` is down from twenty-four typed figures to four — three on the web and one on
iOS. All twenty on Android are gone, counted from the rows underneath them, and three of the four
lies that check was written for lived in that one function: "Active visits 24" over a board of
three, "Available nurses 18" over seven, "Awaiting review 12" over three. Retiring it exposed a
defect in the check itself: a Kotlin string template puts an expression inside a literal, so a regex
matching quote-to-quote read `"Read ${if (flagged == 1) "` as typed prose and found a 1 in it. The
extractor is a scanner now, and it recurses into interpolations rather than skipping them, so
`"${if (late) "24" else "3"}"` is still caught.

**The generated file is in the iOS target.** `CaptureData.swift` is emitted beside its Kotlin twin,
and Gradle compiled the Kotlin one because it globs the source tree while Xcode does not. All four
`project.pbxproj` entries now exist — a `PBXFileReference`, a `PBXBuildFile`, a group `children`
entry and a `PBXSourcesBuildPhase` entry — which is what had been blocking two of the four iOS
quarantines from retiring at all.

**Six clinical iOS screens came off `Form` and `List`, and were looked at.** The assessment, the
Thuso Kit, the laboratory order, the dispatch board, the language screen and the first-run flow,
each captured at the top and the foot, at the default content size and at AccessibilityXXXL, from
the test run's own attachments rather than from a claim that they were fine. `ClinicalFormTests`
holds them there. Two accessibility fixes that had been committed unmeasured are visibly right: the
Kit's "Working as" picker is a full-width control rather than a 34-point tap target, and the
identity switch renders as a switch at its proper size.

**The glass redesign, 8–9 September 2026.** The founder chose a reference and then said of the first
attempt _"this is not the design I sent you"_ — the palette had been taken and the shapes had not.
He then said what he had actually meant: _"something futuristic and having a futuristic glassy feel
with smooth animations… and also putting all functionalities on it from start to finish."_

What landed is a component language rather than a colour scheme. A metric is a status chip floating
_above_ a large thin numeral with a small label beneath — this product did the exact inverse
everywhere, and that inversion was most of why it looked nothing like the reference. Navigation is a
pill row with a circular arrow that inverts on the active row. Separation is a hairline, not a
shadow. And over all of it, frosted glass on a luminous ground.

**Glass has one hard problem and it is solved rather than ignored.** A translucent surface has no
colour of its own — it is whatever is behind it, tinted — so a contrast figure measured against it
is a guess about where the panel sits. Every glass surface therefore declares a _floor_: the tint
composited over the darkest point the ground may reach. Contrast is measured against that, the
ground is built so it cannot go darker, and four things fail the build — an undeclared floor, a
floor that is not actually the composite, a ground darker than the one the floor came from, and a
stylesheet that ignores `prefers-reduced-transparency` or `prefers-reduced-motion`. The check caught
its author's own error on its first run: the wrong colour had been named as the darkest ground.
Charcoal is 16.28:1 on the floor and 14.48:1 on the ground at its worst. 54 pairs, none failing.

The fallback is not a degradation. `backdrop-filter` is expensive on the mid-range Android handsets
this product is for, and where it is missing the glass resolves to the floor — precisely the colour
every ratio was measured against. One agent first put a blur on every chip and button, about forty
compositor layers a screen, and a click began timing out one run in three; it is on six surfaces
now. Glass may never sit on top of text.

**And the flows.** All 96 journeys were walked in a real browser and written down in
`docs/FLOW-COMPLETENESS.md`: 61 complete, 12 blocking, 18 incomplete, 5 rough. Most of the blockers
are closed. A booked visit could not be cancelled at all — and of four visits exactly one had any
controls — while the Cancelled tab promised "the reason and any refund" for a feature that did not
exist. Care plans and the wallet were a single placeholder dialog pressed 28 times across the app,
which meant the two recurring revenue lines the proposal rests on could not be read. The Control
Tower's vetting queue rendered _the nurse's own application form_. The doctor's five outcomes all
opened the same form, and now seven do, each opening what it produces, with the two refusals — a
medical certificate and its extension — rendered on every signed decision. Thuso SOS, one of the
most complete journeys in the build, was reachable only from the fourteenth card inside Explore.

The line held throughout: **a missing next screen is a dead end; a notice saying a capability is not
connected is not.** Otherwise "complete the flows" becomes "pretend it works", which is the one
thing this product cannot do.

**What the glass redesign has not reached: iOS and Android.** Both native apps build green and carry
the new palette, because the tokens are generated into them — but the glass language, the metric
shape and the pill navigation are web only. The two apps and the web app currently look like
relatives rather than the same product.

**The redesign of September 2026.** The founder's words were "not serious and modern, a bit
cartoonish", and the diagnosis was brand drift: the shipped product was a herbal-green system with
no Deep Indigo in it at all, while the funding proposal names Vital Teal, **Deep Indigo**, Mango,
Slate and Soft Grey. Indigo carries the interface now; teal and mango are accents that cannot hold
text on a light ground and are written into `tokens.json` as not-measured with that reasoning beside
them. The decorative serif is gone — a magazine's judgement on a headline that says who is coming to
your house. The web type scale was twenty-five arbitrary sizes with an 11px floor and is thirteen
steps from 13px; Android had twenty-one sizes typed at the call site and eighty-one strings below
the floor; iOS had 410 fixed point sizes that ignored Dynamic Type entirely. All three read one
generated scale now. 38 contrast pairs are computed on every build and none fails.

What that pass also found, by looking at screens rather than at source: a profile button drawn 10px
off the right edge at 390px, a sign-up step number unreadable on its own fill, two family avatars at
3.98:1 and 3.46:1, three horizontal overflows hidden _inside_ `main` where no page-level test could
see them, a Compose status pill breaking "Vitals" across four lines at the largest font scale, two
Android tones that had silently fallen through to the indigo default so no reading in range was ever
teal, a 1MB duplicate logo, no launcher icon at all, and a carousel animating nine bubbles forever
behind a screen that no longer rendered them.

**What is still not done in the redesign.** The deep clinical screens on both native apps — patient
file, capture queue, dispensing, vetting, teleconsultation, programmes — took the systemic pass
(type, spacing, colour, scaling) but not an information-architecture pass; several are still walls of
equal cards. No screen-reader testing has been done anywhere: VoiceOver and TalkBack semantics were
written and inspected, never driven. Nothing has been tested on real hardware or a slow connection.

Six items that used to be on this list have moved, and only as far as they have actually gone.

**Prescription substitution and chronic authorisation** is designed, built on all three platforms, and checked — twenty-five ways of breaking it were tried and every one of them fails the build. **None of its clinical wording has been read by a pharmacist**, and one judgement in it is worth a pharmacist's attention rather than an engineer's: the screen has three substitution classes, not the usual "may / may with telling / must not", because section 22F of the Medicines and Related Substances Act 101 of 1965 makes telling the patient a duty on every substitution — so the lowest tier here is _may be substituted, and the patient is told_, and a silent swap is outside the model rather than at the bottom of it. If that reading of section 22F is wrong, the whole shape of the screen is wrong. The medicines chosen to sit in each class — levothyroxine and a stabilised patient in _must not_, an insulin analogue as a biological, a hydrochlorothiazide supply failure as a pharmacist's judgement — are the same kind of judgement and need the same review. What is also not built: Schedule 5 and above, a formulary, any stock system, an actual notification to a prescriber, and the pharmacy's own dispensing record.

**Employer and sponsor programme administration** is designed, built on all three platforms and checked, with the suppression rule applied in each app from unsuppressed counts rather than handed to them pre-suppressed. **The floor is a judgement, not a standard, and no Information Officer has agreed to it.** Nothing in POPIA names a number; twelve people, a four-fifths dominance ceiling, rounding to five and never leaving exactly one group hidden are a design written down so that it can be argued with. What is not built: any real reporting pipeline, an invoice, an invitation that reaches anybody, and the differencing problem across a series of reports over time — the rounding narrows it and does not close it, and closing it needs somebody who does statistical disclosure control for a living.

**The remaining official languages** are there — all eleven written ones, from one contract, generated into Swift and Kotlin. **A human review of them is not.** Ten of the eleven were drafted by software and have been read by nobody who speaks them, which the app says on every screen that offers one and which a boundary check will not let anybody claim otherwise. What remains is a speaker of each language reading every string in the screen it appears on, and a name, an organisation and a date going into `packages/catalog/locales.json`. **A clinical language review has not started and cannot be started by an engineer**: it needs a clinician who reads the language, and until one signs each language off, clinical wording is English in all of them — which is enforced rather than promised.

**South African Sign Language interpreting** is designed, built on all three platforms and checked — twenty-two ways of breaking it were tried and every one of them fails the build. The guidance in `packages/catalog/locales.json` said what was owed and said that none of it was built; `packages/catalog/interpreting.json` is what carries it out. An interpreter is now the thirteenth vetted party, with six checks of their own and one capability — a build failure if that role is ever granted the patient summary, the record, a result or a protected category, because hearing a consultation is not reading one. The roster carries free hours rather than conclusions, so which hour answers a request is worked out three times from the same numbers; all three `firstFree` signatures can return nothing, and the build fails if one of them stops being able to. A visit that needs an interpreter and has not got one is held rather than dispatched, on the booking screen and in the visit list, in the contract's own word. Cancelling that wait costs nothing at any point and is recorded against MyThuso rather than the patient — both halves checked, because either alone is the failure. On the call the interpreter is the participant the roster already had: when the requirement is on the account they cannot be unticked, the call does not open until they are consented to, and asking them to leave ends the consultation and rebooks it rather than continuing in a language the patient did not choose. The refusals are rendered rather than merely enforced, on the interpreter screen and again on the call roster, which is where somebody would otherwise offer a relative.

**Three things in it are drafted rather than known, and one of them is load-bearing.** The accreditation route is the load-bearing one: MyThuso has taken SATI's accreditation examination as the route a SASL interpreter is checked against, and **nobody at SATI, DeafSA or PanSALB has confirmed that**. If accreditation runs somewhere else, the authority row is wrong and the check hanging off it is the wrong check. The membership-number format is deliberately not asserted — the register accepts the number as it appears on the certificate — because guessing a format is how a real interpreter is told their real number is invalid; that is the one place this feature refuses to be confident. Second, the three modes — in the room, on video, hand over hand for a Deafblind patient — and their relative scarcity are an engineer's guess at how SASL interpreting is actually arranged in South Africa, and the fixture that leaves tactile interpreting with nothing free is a design decision about what the screen must be able to say rather than a claim about supply. Third, **no Deaf South African and no qualified interpreter has read a word of any of it** — not the refusals, not the roster, not the sentence a patient is shown when the app cannot say when somebody will be free. What is also not built: any contact with an interpreter, a real hold on a real visit, an interpreter's own workspace, tactile interpreting as anything other than a mode name, and any of the arrangements for a visit rather than a call — the dispatch note that tells the nurse before she leaves is still guidance rather than a screen.

**Large-text and low-end device testing** is done for the web and for iOS, and measured on every build. The web: 320 px, 200 % zoom, target size and rendered text size, on both viewports. iOS has a test target now — `apps/ios/MyThusoUITests`, XCUITest, run by `xcodebuild test` and by the `ios` job in `.github/workflows/ui-quality.yml` — which drives the home, the booking flow and the Health Passport at the default content size and again at `AccessibilityXXXL`, walks each to the bottom of its content, and measures target size, labels, decorative images announced as elements of their own, anything pushed past the edge of the screen, whether a control laid out clear of the bars can actually be tapped, whether the foot of a nine-screenful page is reachable by scrolling, and whether each string answers the setting at all. It also books a visit end to end and reads the result back: the weekday on every date chip is checked against the date it names by asking the calendar rather than the app, and the visit ends its own service's length after it starts rather than a flat hour — the defect `f0b34df` fixed, now held down on iOS specifically. **It found what reading the screens had not**: every point size in the iOS design system ignored Dynamic Type, so at the largest setting the headings had tripled and the status pills and menu rows were still eleven and fifteen points, and nine controls were under 44 points at the default size, among them the _Change_ link on the last screen before a booking is confirmed and the switch beside the preview consent. Both are fixed. **Screen-reader testing is still not done anywhere**, and neither is testing on real hardware. Android lint runs with its accessibility checks as errors and touch targets and roles on the four newest screens were corrected by hand, but no instrumented test runs. TalkBack, VoiceOver, and a low-end Android phone on a slow connection are all still ahead, and no measurement above is a substitute for any of them. Nor is the iOS suite complete: three screens rather than all of them, one simulator rather than a device, and a `Text` that is visually clipped while its accessibility label stays whole is not something XCUITest can see. The six colour pairs that failed WCAG 2.2 AA are fixed rather than recorded: `--faint`, `--amber` and `--danger` carry the values that had been measured beside them, two teal-on-tint pairs were reclassified as the icons they are, and the focus indicator became two rings with tokens of its own once darkening the warning colour took the old single ring to 2.2:1 on a dark panel. Thirty-two pairs are computed on every build and none fails.

None of these are claimed complete. `docs/ACCESSIBILITY.md` is the longer version of this paragraph.

20 September 2026 — GilbertOne speaks: the founder switched `voice.webSpeech` on, so every reply on the live assistant is read aloud in its own words while the same words stay written on the screen — the caption is the reply itself and nothing switches it off. The microphone's face is A07 (`affect.voiceMoments.capture`), played from the adapter's own open state; the mouth is A10 (`affect.voiceMoments.speaking`), fired from the utterance's own start, word-boundary and end events rather than a timer, and a held safety face refuses it — neverSoften made visible. A browser with no speech recognition is handed the contract's `voice.browserNotice` beside the state line. Motion preferences and neutral refusal/emergency expressions retained. | No new clinical capabilities, authentication or voice permissions. |

21 September 2026 — GilbertOne speaks on the phones too: `voice.nativeSpeech`, decided the day after `voice.webSpeech`, reads every reply aloud on iOS and Android through each platform's own on-device synthesiser — `AVSpeechSynthesizer`/`AVSpeechUtterance` in `GilbertVoice.swift`, `TextToSpeech`/`UtteranceProgressListener` in `GilbertVoice.kt`, both files the only ones on their platform allowed to name either, alongside `SFSpeechRecognizer` and `SpeechRecognizer` — with no network request behind either and nothing recorded, the same on-device rule the microphone has kept since 14 September. `voice.voicePreference`'s order — South African English first, then British, then Australian, then any English voice — is reused rather than restated, applied to whatever the phone's own installed voices or engine locales actually are; a phone with none of the four keeps its own default and none is promised, matching §07's V03 refusal that already governs the web. Unlike the web, where the reply is read aloud with no way to turn it off, both phones carry a speaker button beside the composer field — `gilbert-speech-toggle` on iOS, the same icon button on Android — because a phone is far more often overheard than a desktop browser at a settled address: on by default (matching `voice.webSpeech`'s own default of speaking), muting stops the current sentence immediately and every reply after it, and the choice is held in memory only, resetting the way the composer's own microphone state already does when the screen is reopened. The caption never depends on the voice: every reply is written to the screen whether or not GilbertSpeaker ever runs, on all three platforms. Contract sentences `voice.sentences.muteLabel`, `unmuteLabel` and `speechUnavailable` are new; `voice.nativeSpeech.enabled` is read before either class reaches for a synthesiser at all, the same order `lib/voice.ts` keeps for `voice.webSpeech`. Refusals this adds: no cloud speech provider on either phone (the on-device rule extended, not a new one), and no promise of a South African voice (§07's V03, reused). Covered by `AssistantTests.testTheSpeakerToggleMutesAndUnmutesWithoutAskingForAnything` on iOS, which asserts the toggle opens unmuted, flips its contract-read label on each tap and that reading a reply aloud raises no system permission prompt; boundary checks hold `voice.nativeSpeech`'s provenance, that both `GilbertVoice` files read the flag before reaching for a synthesiser, and that both screens read the mute labels from the contract and call `speaker.speak(...)` rather than typing a label or leaving the mouth unwired.

22 September 2026 — Governed health knowledge federation: the 250-entry catalogue became something an answer can stand on rather than only search. Every entry in `packages/catalog/knowledge` now carries a source object — authority, jurisdiction, retrieved date, an evidence grade drawn from `federation.json`'s own vocabulary — and the eight clinical files carry a `codes` object of SNOMED CT, ICD-11 and LOINC values, 71 entries in all, each verified by hand against the issuing authority's own browser before it was written down; `interactions.json` deliberately carries none, and a `codes` key appearing there is a build failure rather than an omission. `packages/catalog/knowledge/federation.json` allowlists three external sources — the ICD-11 WHO API, openFDA and Europe PMC — and every one of them ships `"active": false` with its endpoint, licence, rate-limit basis, data-residency position and a POPIA s72 note recorded, because no cross-border transfer has been approved and no patient identifier would ever ride a lookup. The adapters in `apps/assistant-api/src/lib/sources` refuse to operate while their source is dark, gate every request through the signed-off rate limit before anything leaves the process, attach provenance to whatever they would return and report unavailability as a fact instead of an exception; they exist as code and are unreachable — `knowledge-federation.ts` above them is the only module allowed to import them, no route imports it, and the boundary checks hold all of that structurally, mutation-proved. Knowledge search results — local and, when a source is ever opened, federated — now come back born with their codes and a structured citation (authority, jurisdiction, evidence grade, dates, licence, URL), rendered as one line under each excerpt by the knowledge tools; the locked `/assistant/v1/knowledge/search` contract is untouched, its `source` still the authority string it always was, with the new fields living above it. Where the federation cannot answer it says so in `federation.json`'s own sentences rather than guessing: nothing found, everything past its review date, two records claiming one code for different subjects, or a question asking for a diagnosis, a prescription, a dose change or the reading of a scan — each an explicit abstention a nurse or doctor can be pointed to. Verification: `scripts/knowledge-codes.mjs` (Verhoeff for SNOMED CT, the LOINC check digit, the ICD-11 MMS format) runs over all nine files on every build; adapter tests mock every byte of HTTP and hold all three dark; federation tests pin dedup, conflict and all four abstentions; and the boundary check refuses a missing source object, a mistyped code, a source flipped active, an adapter without its dark guard, or any file other than `knowledge-federation.ts` reaching for the adapters.

22 September 2026 — GilbertOne written down as what it is: **one API engine, three clients**. A documentation pass, and only that — no deploy ran, no service was switched on, no provider was configured, no clinical gate moved, no contract sentence was reworded, no lock line was touched, nothing was regenerated, and the GilbertOne look and feel, which is fixed, was not restyled in any way. `README.md`, `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`, `docs/PRIVACY-AND-SECURITY.md`, `docs/ROADMAP.md`, `deploy/README.md`, `deploy/RUNBOOK.md`, `CLAUDE.md` and `AGENTS.md` had all grown up around an engine they still introduced as the web app's assistant — as a panel, or as "the second tier" of one — and two of them never named it at all. They now name `apps/assistant-api` as its own service, `packages/catalog/apis/assistant.json` as its contract and the web, iOS and Android applications as its consumers, and they say plainly that the two phones ask it nothing while `unifiedApi` is `enabled: false`. Two stale addresses were corrected in the prose: the turn is `POST /assistant/v1/turn`, with the unversioned `/assistant/turn` asked only where a deployment older than the versioned surface answers that 404. Dated records were annotated rather than rewritten, so what was true when it was written is still readable, and `docs/GilbertOne_Developer_Scope_v1.md` — a supplied source document with its own document-control block — and `docs/governance/DPIA-DRAFT.md`, which pins itself to the commit it was written against, were both left exactly as they were. Verification: `node scripts/check-boundaries.mjs` exits 0, reporting 350 route versions over thirteen engine files, assistant 12, 245 built and 105 proposed, 5 gated built assistant routes, 0 of 12 triage protocols designated, 0 devices in the real-device allowlist and 3 external sources reading `"active": false`; the change is markdown-only, so no source, contract or generated file could drift and the patient entry is unchanged.

## Delivered — golden sets in isiZulu, isiXhosa and Afrikaans for the eval harness, proposed and unreviewed, 27 September 2026 (assistant service only)

The founder's ask of 27 September 2026: clinician-reviewed golden sets in the languages patients use, so that every model change is measured in them. What landed is the contract, the harness and the review process; **no first-language clinician has read a sentence yet**, and the build says so. `docs/governance/GOLDEN-SETS.md` is how a review is done.

| What landed | What it refuses, and what did not move | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **The contract** — `assistant-golden-sets.json`: one set per language (`en` as the reference, `zu`, `xh`, `af`), each with `reviewedBy: null`, `reviewedOn: null`, its `reviewerRole` (a first-language SANC nurse or HPCSA doctor) and 34–38 cases: emergency phrasings the way people say them across every group of `gilbert-emergency-terms.json`, dose, diagnosis, sick-note, role and email refusals, routine cost/booking/nurse questions, handovers, off-topic sentences, and code-switched isiZulu-English, isiXhosa-English and Afrikaans-English. Each case: `id`, `message`, `expect.route` (`emergency`, `refusal:<id>`, `handover`, `in-scope`, `unmatched`) and `expect.language`, a `why` with an English gloss, and `draftedBy: "machine draft, 2026-09-27"`. The file's `routes` section says what "correct" means per route; `status: "proposed"` | **A set with `reviewedBy: null` is run and reported, never required** — the build cannot demand the model pass sentences nobody has verified. No case carries a phone or identity number. The emergency terms are untouched: a sentence the service misses is a finding for the list's own changelog, never an edit from here. **What the first run found** (printed on every `npm test`, not restated as numbers here): the English reference misses four drafts — "my chest is tight" (the listed term is `chest tight`; the service's substring matcher does not gap the way the phones' matcher does), "ending it all" (no crisis term for it), "how much Panado can I give my 3 year old" (the dosing pattern in `refusals.ts` asks for *should I give*, not *can I give*), and the sick note (no refusal names one). These are findings about the matcher's reach and the detector, not about the sentences; a review does not change them, it makes them count.

**What did not move.** No route, lock line, event or native file. `packages/gilbertone`, `gilbert-emergency-terms.json`, `assistant.json`, the refusal patterns and the language detector are untouched: every gap above is reported here and in the test output, and fixed nowhere in this change. Nothing under `apps/web` or `deploy/`. The patient's first load is unaffected.

## Delivered — symptom intake: notes for the nurse, 28 September 2026

The founder's ask of 28 September 2026: a patient told GilbertOne "I have a headache" and it could not answer her. GilbertOne does not do diagnosis, but it needs to ask the pertinent questions so that they reach the nurse assigned to the patient, already asked, before the visit. This is **not triage**: it sets no priority, no disposition, names no cause and gives no advice. It is a structured set of notes the patient answers for the nurse, one deterministic question per turn, every sentence a contract's.

| What landed | What it refuses, and what did not move | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **The intake contract** — `symptom-intake.json`: eleven symptom groups (headache, stomach, fever, cough-cold, dizziness, nausea, back-joint, skin, tiredness, urinary, and the general "not feeling well"), each with patient-typed triggers and two or three questions of its own after five common ones (since when, how bad, better or worse, what was used, long-term conditions); chips or text; the offer, the yes/no words and chips, the stop word, the closing, the way to a nurse, the unmatched-inside sentence; `review.reviewedBy: null` with the unreviewed sentence; the notes card's title and `{question}: {answer}` line; `platforms: ["web"]`; eighteen message fixtures and one whole-flow fixture | **The emergency terms are checked on the opening message and on every answer before the intake reads it, the refusal policies next, the intake last** — written as `order.rule`, and the file carries no red-flag rule because that is the ratified triage protocol's job. No key anywhere named `priority`, `disposition`, `urgency`, `careSetting` or `diagnosis`. No question or option carries a clinical instruction or a digit while nobody clinical has signed; the day `reviewedBy` is not null it must be a registration in `vetting.json`'s own format. No trigger is or contains an emergency term; no trigger is one of `assistant.json`'s; every group is opened by a fixture | `packages/catalog/symptom-intake.json` |
| **The package** — `packages/gilbertone/src/intake.ts`: `intakeGroupFor` (longest trigger, stems adjacent, tie to the first group), `beginIntake`, `currentQuestion`, `answerIntake` (immutable; the stop word as a whole message ends it; the engine's emergency classifier and the escalation ruleset are asked of every answer and end it with `{kind:"emergency"}`), `intakeConsent`, `summaryRows`, `intakeReviewSentence`; tests replay the contract's fixtures | **No network, no model, no environment variable**, the package's own rule. The module types no sentence; it reads them | `packages/gilbertone/src/intake.ts`, `intake.test.ts` |
| **The web** — `assistant.json` gains the `intake` question (patient-only, web-only, situations group, the offer's own trigger words), `answers.intake` (state), a routine spoken register and a warm face; `lib/assistant.ts` decides the intake in `send()` after the emergency words and the refusals and before anything is unmatched, so a complaint the groups know never reaches the one reply the panel waits on the service for; `continueIntake` answers into an open intake — emergency words first, then yes/no, then the package — and `activeIntake` reads it off the last turn alone; the panel draws the offer with its two chips, a question with its options as 44px buttons or a hint to type, and the notes card (question beside answer) with the closing, the review disclosure, Copy the notes (the person's own clipboard; nothing stored) and the existing way to a nurse; the intake chip joins the situations row | **A headache never shows the waiting dots** (the dots are gated on the unmatched kind, and the intake comes before it). An intake offer on a message no question matched still reports the matcher's `unmatched` outcome — the phones' word for the same shared fixture — so `fixtures.messages` are untouched and still pass on all three platforms; the phones themselves render nothing of this yet. The intake question consumes its whole message, so nothing is left unread beside the ambulance numbers | `apps/web/src/lib/assistant.ts`, `features/Assistant.tsx`, `features/assistant.css`, `packages/catalog/assistant.json` |

Siri and Bixby are the references on behaviour." Built in two phases the same day: the contract, the machine, the web driver and the native data files first; the panel's wiring second.

The founder's ask of 29 September: "there were mapbox and live triage features … please wire all those
features and make them work." The map had drawn OpenFreeMap streets behind a switch that started off for
everyone, so the founder had only ever seen the schematic. Now the switch starts where the surface says —
on for a dispatcher and a nurse, off for a patient — and Mapbox is a provider a build may choose by token,
never by edit and never with a value in this repository. Nothing about what a tile request may carry
changed: the viewport, the address that asked and the time, and never a pin. The patient entry measured
the same way as before: **252.36 kB** across 15 files (gzip -9, every asset `dist/index.html` references)
against 251.85 kB on the same tree before this change — the 0.5 kB is 0.27 kB of the map's own contract
and code in the Workspace chunk and 0.12 kB in the SOS chunk from a change in flight beside this one.
The staff chunks the streets ride in: `TileMap` 282.4 kB, `maplibre-gl-worker` 145.6 kB, both still
behind the one dynamic import.

| What landed | What it refuses, and why | Files |
|---|---|---|
| **A default per surface.** `geography.json` `rendering.tiles.defaultBySurface: { staff: "on", patient: "off" }` with its why; `LiveMap` takes `surface` (a caller that does not say is a patient's); Dispatch and the care visit pass `staff`, Arrival passes `patient`. The switch stays, the disclosure stays beside it naming the provider, and a staff screen says why streets started on (`startedOnSentence`) | `tiles.default` stays off and the patient's default is held to off by a check; only the two staff screens may pass `staff`, and a third fails the build until somebody adds it deliberately. Nothing is remembered on any surface — the not-remembered sentence is shown only once the switch has been moved away from the surface's own default, and says which way it goes back | `packages/catalog/geography.json`, `apps/web/src/lib/geography.ts`, `apps/web/src/map/LiveMap.tsx`, `features/Dispatch.tsx`, `features/CareVisit.tsx`, `features/Arrival.tsx` |
| **Mapbox by token.** `rendering.alternateSources` names the entry and the key that chooses it (`VITE_MAPBOX_TOKEN`); its endpoint, origins, licence, credit, usage policy, label font and hidden layers are in `packages/catalog/map-providers.json`, read only by the tile chunk. `lib/geography.ts` picks Mapbox when the token is set at build time and OpenFreeMap otherwise; `map/mapboxRequests.ts` rewrites the style's `mapbox://` sources, sprites, glyphs and styles to `api.mapbox.com` and appends the token to `api.mapbox.com` and `*.tiles.mapbox.com` requests; the credit under the map is what the tile map reports it drew with | The style URL is the https form, because MapLibre loads nothing from `mapbox://`. ## Delivered — the case pathway: GilbertOne gathers, the nurse decides where, the doctor decides what, 29 September 2026 (web only)

The founder's ask of 28–29 September 2026: one complaint wired end to end so the product can be demonstrated responding and escalating — "choose one thing like headache and we link it to a high blood pressure which then gets escalated to a nurse and then the doctor … determine a case if it will need online or physical treatment". The honest design is a **Case** that GilbertOne gathers, a nurse who decides where the patient is seen, and a doctor who decides what it is. **Not triage**: guided triage stays refused behind a ratified protocol, and this codebase refuses a seeded sign-off, so the pathway is a **draft protocol that suggests and a nurse confirms**, named as a draft on every screen that shows it. The script is `docs/governance/CASE-PATHWAY-DEMO.md`.

| **Knowledge-linked questions.** `symptom-intake.json`'s headache group gains `questionsFrom` — the seven entries in `knowledge/conditions.json` that list headache (cond-002, 008, 024, 025, 041, 043, 062) — and ten questions of its own, each naming the entries it draws on in `drawsOn` (where; light or noise; sick or vomited; sight; dizzy; nosebleeds; fever, chills or a sore throat; a malaria area; a knock — kept with `keptBecause`, since the base has no head-injury entry; usual blood pressure or pills for it); the flow fixture answers all fifteen; the review pack's F4 prints the derivation | Every question names a source or says why not; every entry is drawn on; no question or option carries an emergency feature (`case.json#findings.emergencyFeatures`) or an emergency term — an answer naming one is answered by the emergency words first, as before. A derived group may ask up to fifteen with the common five; a written group still five to eight. **Open.** The routes are proposed, not bound on the engine runtime: an engine store may hold references only, and a case's answers and readings are Passport entries the engine would read through the gateway — a day's work that was not started. Three emergency features (a stiff neck, confusion, weakness on one side) are not in `gilbert-emergency-terms.json`; adding them is a versioned change with a clinical reviewer. No clinician has reviewed the derived questions or the pathway (review pack F4). The phones render no case. The nurse's kit reading is a pair she types off a fictional instrument, not a paired capture.

Two Lovable exports exist. Waves 1–6 (2a, 2b, 3a, 3b, 4a–4e, 5a, 5b and the closing CI document) were built
from `designs/mythuso-claude-handoff.zip` — 35 files, downloaded 28 September 18:56 — whose extracted copy
and manifest live at `packages/brand/lovable-handoff/`. A second, larger export,
`mythuso-full-project.zip` — 203 files, 3,702,477 bytes uncompressed, internal stamp 2026-09-29 11:59,
downloaded 29 September 12:07:41 — arrived after commit `61310305` (10:57:15 +0200) and after the deploy
whose bundle carries `Last-Modified: Tue, 29 Sep 2026 08:58:09 GMT`, so no session could have built from
it. It carries what the first did not: 68 role routes (patient 30, nurse 19, doctor 15, partner 4), 17
showcase screens totalling 2,651 lines, the `ai-elements` set, a Radix-backed `ui/` kit,
`.lovable/design-system.json` and `.lovable/system.md` (the Careline design language). Its `theme.css` is
byte-identical to the first export's (SHA-256 prefix `9ecaa125efa3bc61258c`), so the tokens waves 1–6
implemented are the same tokens this export carries; what is new in it is layout and motion, not colour.

## Delivered — the Lovable export's layouts, navigation and missing screens, drawn in the live theme, 30 September 2026 (web only)

The founder asked on 30 September to _"make sure the new changes of Lovable are all there but in the current theme"_.
Four read-only audits then compared the export (`designs/mythuso-full-project.zip`) with the live app element by
element, one each for the patient, the nurse and the map, the doctor and the partner, and the landing page with
the Control Tower and the assistant. They agreed on one finding, and it contradicts the record above and in
`docs/design-review/LOVABLE-FULL-ALIGNMENT.md`: **the words and the refusals matched, but the layouts, the
navigation and several whole screens the export draws were not in the live app**, including screens that record
called _built_ which a person in the role could not reach. Seven builders closed the buildable gaps, each in its
own files in one tree. "In the current theme" means the tokens and the `.ui-*` components: nothing from the
export's stack (Tailwind, Radix, TanStack, Supabase, `mapbox-gl`, `recharts`, `motion`) entered `apps/web`, and
no dependency was added. The export's arrangement was taken; its behaviour was not, wherever it draws a number,
a person, a message or a clinical reading that no contract holds.

Verified on the finished tree: `npm run check` green (every workspace's typecheck and `check-boundaries.mjs`);
`npm test`: the eleven node suites pass (2,829 tests, none failed) and the journeys ran **1,331 passed, 26 skipped and 7 failed** on both viewports; six of the seven were journeys reaching a screen this work moved (`care-safety-reads.spec.ts:47` on both viewports, `household.spec.ts:71`, `sponsor.spec.ts:44`, `:66` and `:80`), corrected in how they reach it with every assertion kept, and the seventh (`control-tower-portal.spec.ts:457` on a phone, a chip lifting under the pointer) passes on its own — those four files re-run together pass 76 of 76; iOS `BUILD SUCCEEDED` and Android `assembleDebug` + `lintDebug` `BUILD SUCCESSFUL`. **The patient's
first load: 265.31 kB across 15 files**, measured the documented way, against **259.19 kB** for what
`mythuso.co.za` served the same morning measured the same way, and the 282.16 kB ceiling. The 6.12 kB is the
patient's own new sidebar, top bar and home; the staff chrome's rules were first appended to `shells.css`, which
the patient downloads, and were moved to `shells/staff-chrome.css` on the staff chunk before this was measured.
The landing entry: **125.75 kB across 17 files** against 123.51 kB live, the hero's guide card, the impact card
and the footer columns.

## Delivered — knowledge sources: fourteen assessed and dark, twelve turned away, and a link pasted is only a proposal, 1 October 2026 (web; contract)

The founder asked for more first-aid, skin and consumer-health sources to make GilbertOne's photo skin-check and
first-aid answers stronger. The licences were read on their owners' pages, and the finding that matters most is
uncomfortable: **no openly licensed, clinically authoritative first-aid or skin text exists that a commercial South
African service may draw on as published**, and none in isiZulu, Afrikaans or Sesotho. Every source below is dark;
every one waits on two signatures nobody can give yet. `docs/governance/KNOWLEDGE-SOURCES.md` is the assessment.

| What landed | What it refuses, and what did not move | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |

A changelog records both versions | **Every source `"active": false`; none has an adapter but the first three, and no runtime reads the new ones.** The three existing licence strings, which flow into citations, are unchanged. `licenceVerdicts` gives seven verdicts; `permission-required` opens only with `licensing.permissionRef`, and `non-commercial-only`, `no-reuse`, `outside-licence-scope` and `not-assessed` never open | `packages/catalog/knowledge/federation.json` |
| **`assessedNotAdmitted`: twelve publishers turned away with their reasons** — the NHS content API (UK users and England's direct care only), WHO fact sheets and IRIS, DermNet (and its ban on AI use of its images), Dermnet.com, the AAD, Cochrane, gov.za, Health-e, Hesperian, Healthdirect, Mayo Clinic and Merck Manuals | A licence that excludes a commercial service is not cured by proposing it again (`proposal-assessed-and-not-admitted`); a host is admitted or turned away, never both | `packages/catalog/knowledge/federation.json` |
| **Governance · Knowledge sources**, a new tab behind its own dynamic import: the two signatories and what each signs, every source with its verdict and "Awaiting two signatures", the turned-away register, and a field to paste a link | **A pasted link is a proposed source, never knowledge** (`a-link-is-not-knowledge`): held in the screen's React state alone, never fetched, opened, linked to or stored, gone when the screen is left.
